title: Shloka 53
subtitle: From all the diagrams and all the scriptures to the beloved of the gracious one

namas.translation: A drawn diagram is only lines until she inhabits it as its living self.

morphology.note: ātmikā is the feminine of the -ka derivative ātmaka, and it is the suffix that supplies the having; the base compound is sarvayantrātman. Read the other way the name is a bahuvrīhi, she whose self is every yantra.

namas.translation: Named from Maheśvara himself, she is the sovereign power without which the great lord would not act.

morphology.note: vṛddhi derivative on maheśvara; the members can also be taken directly as mahā- and īśvarī

namas.translation: Of all the goddesses she is the one from whom the title itself derives.
As Mahālakṣmī she is fortune at its source, not the small luck that comes and goes.
She is dear to Śiva under the name he bears when he is merciful.

compound.gloss: the beloved of the gracious one

children.gloss: the gracious or merciful one, Śiva

commentary.meaning: Seven names, and the verse changes gear halfway through. It opens at the end of a long run of names beginning sarva-, all: she is the self of every ritual diagram and the form of every tantra, and since the name immediately before these calls her the very being of every mantra, the three instruments of the tradition are claimed for her across the line break. Then comes manonmanī, mind beyond mind, and the run of totalities stops, because it has reached the place where the faculty that totals things up gives out. The second line then abandons long compounds altogether for four bare titles of four syllables each: great sovereign, great goddess, great Lakṣmī, and last — after all that magnitude — beloved of Mṛḍa, the gracious one, which is Śiva under the name he is given when he is being kind. The verse travels from everything, through the end of thinking, to somebody's wife. It is a descent, and it is meant to be.
commentary.history:
Yantra and tantra are ordinary Sanskrit nouns before they are technical ones. Yantra, from √yam, to hold or restrain, with the instrumental suffix -tra, is a device for holding something in place — a machine, a lock, a water-lifting engine — and in this tradition the geometrical figure that holds a deity. Tantra, from √tan, to stretch, is the warp stretched on a loom and then any framework, and finally a class of revealed text with the practice it prescribes. The two names here take these in opposite grammatical directions, and the difference is worth catching. Sarvayantrātmikā makes her the ātman of the diagrams, their self or animating principle, so that the drawing is a body and she is what is in it. Sarvatantrarūpā makes the scriptures her rūpa, her form, so that the corpus is the outside of her rather than the inside. Interior and exterior of the same claim, in that order.

Elsewhere the hymn will call her mahātantrā and mahāyantrā, she whose tantra and diagram are the great ones. It is worth noticing that these are different assertions. The mahā- names single out one system as the complete one against the partial others; the sarva- names here take in every system there is, including the partial ones. A litany of a thousand names can afford both, and the fact that it makes both is characteristic. Absorption and supremacy are the two moves available to a tradition that wants to claim everything, and this hymn declines to choose.

Manonmanī is a technical term of the Śaiva tantric schools and does not mean simply a peaceful mind. It belongs to the analysis of the sound of a mantra as it thins out into silence. Above the audible syllable the tradition counts a ladder of increasingly subtle phases — the point, the half-moon, the resonance, the end of resonance, and beyond them still the levels called samanā, with mind, and unmanā, without it or beyond it. Unmanā is the last, where sound has passed out of anything that could be heard and mind out of anything that could be thought. Manonmanī is manas joined to that word: the transmental condition of mind itself, and in the Śaiva texts also a proper name of Śiva's power. Placed where it is, immediately after two claims of universal extent, it does the work of a hinge. Everything can be listed until the lister stops.

The three great-names that follow are the hymn doing something a sahasranāma is peculiarly good at. Māheśvarī is a vṛddhi derivative from Maheśvara, and it is also the name of one of the mother goddesses, the mātṛkās, who is Śiva's power in the standard set and rides his bull. Mahālakṣmī belongs to a different lineage entirely: Viṣṇu's consort, the goddess of the Śrī Sūkta, and in the systematisation of the Devī Māhātmya one of the three great forms under which the whole work is organised. To place her here, unremarked, among Śaiva titles, is a doctrinal act carried out by list rather than by argument. Neither goddess is being compared to Lalitā. Both are being named as her.

Mṛḍa is the last word of the verse and the mildest. It comes from √mṛḍ, to be gracious or to show mercy, and it is one of the euphemistic names of Rudra, the placating epithet used of a god who is otherwise addressed as an archer whose arrows are disease. The Vedic hymns to Rudra are full of the imperative of this root: be gracious to us. Pāṇini's grammar treats mṛḍa as one of a small closed group of divine names — with indra, varuṇa, bhava, śarva and rudra — whose feminines take a special augment, which is how Indrāṇī, Bhavānī, Rudrāṇī and Mṛḍānī are formed; so mṛḍa has its own goddess already built into the language. The verse chooses not to use that form. It names him instead, and calls her his beloved, ending a catalogue of sovereignty on a word that means nothing but kindness.
commentary.practice:
The two lines of this verse are shaped quite differently and should not be recited at the same pace. The first is two long compounds and a shorter name, six syllables plus six plus four; the second is four names of four syllables each, laid down evenly. The natural effect is an acceleration into the second line, and it is worth letting that happen rather than resisting it, because the sense does the same thing: elaborate descriptions giving way to bare titles.

There is a trap in the first line that catches almost everyone. The quarter ends at the eighth syllable, which falls inside sarvatantrarūpā — after sar-va, with tan-tra-rū-pā belonging to the second quarter. Do not breathe there and do not let the name break in half. The pause in this verse comes at the halfway mark, after manonmanī, and nowhere else.

Manonmanī hides a seam. It is manas plus unmanī; the final s of manas becomes o before a voiced sound, so the o you hear in ma-no-nma-nī is the product of a join rather than a vowel of either word. Knowing this also fixes the nm cluster that follows, which is dental n released directly into labial m with no vowel between them.

The clusters in this verse are its real difficulty. Ntr appears twice, in yantra and tantra: dental n, dental t, then r, three separate articulations with nothing swallowed. Tm in ātmikā is dental t followed by m, again with no intruding vowel. Śv in māheśvarī is the palatal sibilant, made further forward than the retroflex ṣ, plus v. And kṣm in mahālakṣmī is the hardest thing here, three consonants at three different places of articulation — velar k, retroflex ṣ, labial m — which must be got through without an English speaker's instinctive vowel appearing in the middle.

The join between the last two names is instructive because it disappears in ritual use. In the shloka you say mahālakṣmīr mṛḍapriyā: the visarga that ends mahālakṣmīḥ turns into r before the voiced m that follows. That r belongs to neither name. When the verse is broken up for archanā the two are separate — mahālakṣmyai namaḥ, mṛḍapriyāyai namaḥ — and the r is simply gone. Reciters who have learned the shloka first often carry it across by mistake.

The archanā forms otherwise sort into the two familiar patterns. The ā-stems take -āyai: sarvayantrātmikāyai, sarvatantrarūpāyai, mṛḍapriyāyai. The ī-stems take -yai: manonmanyai, māheśvaryai, mahādevyai, mahālakṣmyai.

What the verse asks is mostly a matter of not stopping early. Its first half is the kind of statement that invites a certain expansiveness of feeling — she is all diagrams, all scriptures, the state past thought — and a reciter can be forgiven for wanting to rest there. The verse does not rest there. It goes on to name her as the wife of a god called the gracious one, and the last word of thirty-two syllables of grandeur is a term of affection. The proportions are the instruction.

crossReferences.translation: Not conscious of what is within, not conscious of what is without, not conscious of both, not a mass of consciousness, neither conscious nor unconscious; unseen, not to be dealt with, not to be grasped, without a mark, unthinkable, not to be pointed at; whose essence is the certainty of the one self, in which the unfolded world comes to rest; quiet, benign, without a second — that they hold to be the fourth. That is the self. That is what is to be known.
crossReferences.relevance: The classical statement of a condition described only by what it excludes, and the nearest thing in the older literature to what manonmanī names. The word acintya, unthinkable, is the Upaniṣad's version of the hymn's beyond-mind. One further coincidence is worth noticing: the passage calls that state śiva, benign, using the adjective before it became a proper name — the same softening move the verse makes at its close with mṛḍa.

crossReferences.translation: Gold-coloured, tawny, garlanded in silver and gold, bright as the moon, made of gold — that Lakṣmī, O knower of all that is born, bring to me.
crossReferences.relevance: The opening of the hymn that established Lakṣmī's vocabulary, and a reminder of how far she stands from this one's world. Here she is invoked through Agni for wealth, in a Vedic supplementary hymn with no goddess-theology behind it. By the time of the sahasranāma she has become a name of somebody else, and the seamlessness of that absorption in the second line of this verse is the point: no argument is offered, and none is felt to be needed.

crossReferences.iast: aham ātmā guḍākeśa sarvabhūtāśayasthitaḥ | aham ādiś ca madhyaṃ ca bhūtānām anta eva ca ||
crossReferences.translation: I am the self, Guḍākeśa, seated in the inmost part of every being. I am the beginning and the middle of beings, and their end as well.
crossReferences.relevance: The grammar of sarvayantrātmikā in an older and more famous form. To be the ātman of a class of things is not to be one of them or the sum of them but to be what they have instead of a self of their own. The Gītā says it of beings and the hymn says it of diagrams, which is a stranger claim: a drawn figure is being credited with the kind of interior that only a living thing normally has.

references.title: Vāc: The Concept of the Word in Selected Hindu Tantras
references.author: André Padoux, tr. Jacques Gontier (SUNY Press, 1990)
references.note: The indispensable book for manonmanī. Padoux sets out the whole ladder of phases through which mantric sound is held to rise and dissolve, from the audible syllable up through the resonance to samanā and unmanā, and explains why a tradition obsessed with speech would locate its highest state in the exhaustion of speech. Nothing else in English does this properly.

references.title: Encountering the Goddess: A Translation of the Devī-Māhātmya and a Study of Its Interpretation
references.author: Thomas B. Coburn (SUNY Press, 1991)
references.note: Read this for the mechanics of absorption, which is what the second line of this verse is doing. Coburn is precise about how the Devī Māhātmya gathers separate goddesses into one and about the later scheme that made Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī and Mahāsarasvatī the organising triad of the text — the background against which Mahālakṣmī can appear in a Śaiva hymn without comment.

references.title: The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation
references.author: ed. and tr. Patrick Olivelle (Oxford University Press, 1998)
references.note: For the Māṇḍūkya passage quoted above, in a translation that refuses to smooth the negations into something comfortable. Olivelle's notes are also the best short guide to how much later Vedāntic and tantric vocabulary was read back into these very short texts.

references.title: Śrī Sūkta
references.author: a khila or supplementary hymn transmitted with the Ṛgveda
references.note: Fifteen verses, chanted at Lakṣmī worship all over India and short enough to learn in an afternoon. Worth reading in full here because it shows what Lakṣmī meant before she was absorbed: gold, cattle, food, the absence of her sister Alakṣmī. The great in Mahālakṣmī is doing a great deal of work.

references.note: Look up mṛḍ and mṛḍa. The entry makes plain that the name is built on a verb of showing mercy and is used of Rudra precisely where he is being asked not to harm — which is the whole content of the last name in this verse and is invisible in any translation that renders mṛḍapriyā simply as beloved of Śiva.
